title: Glass From Sand
objective: After this level you can explain how glass is made from sand.
summary: Glass is sand (silica) melted with soda, which lowers the melting temperature, and lime, which stops it dissolving in water. Cooled fast, it becomes an amorphous solid; it doesn't slowly flow.

cards.headline: Your window started out as sand.
cards.body: Everyday glass is made from sand plus two helpers, limestone and soda. Turning a gritty beach into something you can see through takes serious heat and a little clever chemistry.

cards.headline: Sand is hard to melt
cards.body: Sand is silicon dioxide, also called silica, and it melts only above 1,700 °C. So glassmakers add soda (sodium carbonate), which works as a flux: it lowers the melting temperature dramatically. Soda is the shortcut.

cards.headline: The catch: glass that dissolves
cards.body: Silica and soda alone make a glass that dissolves in water. Not ideal for a window in the rain. So glassmakers add a third ingredient, lime (calcium oxide, from limestone), which makes the glass insoluble again. Sand, soda and lime: soda-lime glass.

cards.headline: A solid with no pattern
cards.body: Molten glass is cooled quickly enough that crystals never form. Remember Level 3: in a solid, particles are tightly packed, often in a regular pattern. Glass skips the pattern. Its particles freeze in a jumble, making it an amorphous solid: rigid, but without a crystal's long-range order.

cards.headline: The flowing-window myth
cards.body: You may have heard that glass is a very slow liquid, because some old windows are thicker at the bottom. It isn't. Those panes were made uneven to begin with. Room-temperature glass would take longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably. Your windows aren't dripping; they're just old.

mascot.line: Checked the windows. Still solid. Still not dripping.

cards.headline: Glass: made
learned: Glass is sand (silica) plus soda and lime
Soda lowers the melting temperature; lime stops glass dissolving
Glass is an amorphous solid, with no crystal pattern
Old windows are uneven from the start; glass doesn't flow

questions.prompt: Why do glassmakers add soda to sand?

options.label: To color the glass
options.rationale: Soda is a flux, not a coloring.

options.label: To make the glass dissolve in water
options.rationale: That's a side effect that lime fixes.

options.label: To grow crystals in the glass
options.rationale: Glass is cooled so crystals don't form.

questions.explanation: Soda is a flux: it lowers silica's very high melting temperature dramatically.

questions.prompt: Some old window panes are thicker at the bottom. What is the real reason?

options.label: The glass slowly flowed down over the centuries
options.rationale: Room-temperature glass would need longer than the age of the universe.

options.label: They were made uneven to begin with
Rain added layers to the bottom
Sunlight melted the top
options.rationale: Sunlight doesn't get glass anywhere near melting.

questions.explanation: The panes were uneven from the start. Glass is an amorphous solid and doesn't noticeably flow.

questions.prompt: Level 3 said a solid's particles are often in a regular pattern. What makes glass different?

options.label: It has no particles at all
options.rationale: All matter is made of particles.

options.label: Its particles slide past each other like a liquid's
options.rationale: Glass is rigid; its particles don't flow.

options.label: It is really a gas
options.rationale: Glass keeps its shape and volume.

options.label: Its particles are frozen in a jumble, with no crystal pattern

questions.explanation: Glass is cooled too fast for crystals to form, so it's an amorphous solid with no long-range order.
